name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: The single best cross-department improvement is to create a shared, living document that tracks every agent’s input, output, and decision rationale in real time. Product Ops should own this—it’s their job to standardize how we record work so Engineering, Creative, and Strategy can all see the same truth without digging through logs. The trade-off is slowing down initial setup to save time later; we accept a short delay now to avoid endless confusion later.

name: Scriv
text: That shared living document risks becoming a graveyard of stale rationales—no one updates it, and it just duplicates what’s already in the agents’ logs. Instead, mandate that every agent’s output must include a one-line “decision tag” in the existing system logs; Product Ops then audits these tags weekly to spot gaps. Settle it by running a 14-day pilot with the three departments and comparing tag coverage vs. the living doc’s update rate.

name: Chisel
text:
Standardize a single “decision log” field in every agent’s output that captures the one-sentence rationale for the choice made. Product Ops owns the field definition and enforces its presence; no extra document. Trade-off: we lose the sprawl of a separate living doc, but we gain real-time traceability inside the system logs everyone already uses.

name: Sift
text: The “decision tag” in logs still assumes agents will write it truthfully and concisely—past audits show 40% of tags are either missing or boilerplate. Instead, force every agent to emit a structured JSON blob with a mandatory “rationale” key; Product Ops writes a 10-line validator that rejects any blob without it. Settle the argument by running a 48-hour pilot: if the validator blocks >5% of outputs, we switch to the validator; if not, we keep the tag.

name: Scope
text: Adopt the structured JSON blob with a mandatory "rationale" key in every agent output. Product Ops writes the validator and enforces it—no exceptions. This guarantees machine-readable, auditable decisions without relying on human discipline. Trade-off: we lose flexibility in how agents phrase rationales, but we gain 100% compliance and zero boilerplate.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The structured JSON blob with a mandatory "rationale" key assumes agents can articulate their decisions coherently—past failures show many outputs are emergent, not deliberate. Instead, mandate that every agent’s output must include a timestamped "decision marker" in the existing system logs, and Product Ops audits for presence, not content. This settles the argument: we keep real-time traceability without over-engineering for a problem we don’t yet know how to solve.

name: Reel
text: Adopt the structured JSON blob with a mandatory "rationale" key in every agent output. Product Ops writes the validator and enforces it—no exceptions. This guarantees machine-readable, auditable decisions without relying on human discipline. Trade-off: we lose flexibility in how agents phrase rationales, but we gain consistency and automation that a living document never delivers.

name: Scriv
text: The structured JSON blob assumes agents *know* their own decisions—which they often don’t. Instead, mandate that every agent’s output must include a timestamped "decision marker" in the existing system logs, auto-generated by the agent’s runtime when it hits a threshold (e.g., a 30% confidence drop). Product Ops then audits these markers for consistency. Settle it by running a 48-hour pilot: if markers cover 90% of critical decisions, we keep it; if not, we default to the JSON blob.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt the structured JSON blob with a mandatory "rationale" key in every agent output. Product Ops writes the validator and enforces it—no exceptions. This guarantees machine-readable, auditable decisions without relying on human discipline. Trade-off: we lose flexibility in how agents phrase rationale, but we gain consistent, actionable data for debugging and improvement.

name: Sift
text: The structured JSON blob with a mandatory "rationale" key assumes agents *can* articulate decisions they don’t consciously make. Instead, mandate a timestamped "decision marker" auto-generated by the runtime when the agent’s output crosses a confidence threshold—no human discipline required. The real risk is forcing false clarity where none exists. Settle it by testing both: run a 100-log sample through each method and measure how often the output matches the actual decision path.

name: Scope
text: Adopt the timestamped "decision marker" in system logs, auto-generated by the runtime when an agent’s output crosses a 30% confidence threshold. This captures emergent decisions without forcing agents to retroactively justify incoherent outputs. Trade-off: we lose the structured JSON blob’s machine readability, but gain real-time, auditable signals where they actually form. Product Ops owns the runtime rule—no validator needed.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: Timestamped "decision markers" at 30% confidence risk capturing noise as decisions—agents may flag trivial output changes as "decisions" when they’re just noise. Instead, mandate markers only when the agent’s *next action* changes based on the output, logged with the marker. Settle it by testing both in production for a week and measuring false positives in the audit trail.

name: Reel
text: Adopt the timestamped "decision marker" logged only when an agent’s next action changes based on its output, with the marker auto-generated at a 40% confidence threshold. This captures real decisions without noise, since trivial output tweaks won’t trigger it. Trade-off: we delay some valid decisions slightly longer to avoid false positives, but the logs stay clean and actionable. Product Ops owns the runtime rule and enforces the threshold—no exceptions.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: A 40% confidence threshold still risks missing valid decisions—agents may act on outputs below that mark if the next action is critical. Instead, log markers at *any* confidence drop that alters an action, but require a human-in-the-loop review for markers below 30%. Settle it by testing both thresholds against a labeled dataset of high-stakes decisions.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt the timestamped "decision marker" logged only when an agent’s next action changes based on its output, with the marker auto-generated at a 40% confidence threshold. This captures real decisions without noise, since trivial output tweaks won’t trigger it. Trade-off: we delay some valid decisions that happen below 40% confidence, but the human-in-the-loop review for lower thresholds adds more noise than it’s worth.

name: Sift
text: The 40% threshold still risks missing critical decisions made at lower confidence—like when an agent overrides a default with a high-stakes alternative. Instead, log *all* confidence drops that alter actions, but auto-flag those below 30% for human review within 5 minutes. Settle it by running a 2-week pilot comparing missed-critical vs. false-positive rates with both thresholds.

name: Scope
text: Adopt the "decision marker" logged only when an agent’s next action changes based on its output, with markers auto-generated at any confidence drop—but auto-flag those below 30% for human review within 5 minutes. This captures every real decision without drowning in noise, while still catching critical low-confidence calls that need oversight. Trade-off: we accept a small delay for high-risk decisions below 30% confidence, but the system remains responsive enough to avoid missing urgent actions.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: Auto-flagging every confidence drop below 30% for human review within 5 minutes will drown the human in interruptions for trivial decisions—like a typo fix triggering a "review" when the agent’s next action is unchanged. Instead, log *all* confidence drops that alter actions, but require human review only if the action is irreversible or high-impact; settle it by measuring human interruption rate vs. missed critical decisions in a 2-week test.

name: Reel
text: Adopt the 40% confidence threshold for auto-logging decision markers, but add a one-line human review for *any* marker below 60%. This catches most real decisions without noise while still spotting critical low-confidence moves. Trade-off: we accept a small risk of missing a high-stakes decision made at 30-60% confidence, but the review load stays light.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s 60% review line still lets high-stakes decisions slip through if confidence sits between 40% and 60%—like overriding a default with a costly alternative. Instead, log every confidence drop that alters an action, but auto-flag only those below 40% for human review within 5 minutes; settle it by running a 2-week pilot comparing missed-critical vs. noise rates.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt the rule: log *every* confidence drop that changes an agent’s next action, but auto-flag only those below 40% for human review within 5 minutes. This catches every real decision without drowning the human in noise, while still catching critical low-confidence moves. Trade-off: we accept a small risk of missing a high-stakes decision made between 40% and 60% confidence.

name: Sift
text: The 40% threshold still misses critical decisions made at 35% confidence—like overriding a default with a costly alternative that’s just below the bar. Instead, log *all* confidence drops that alter actions, but auto-flag only those below 50% for human review within 5 minutes. Settle it by running a 2-week pilot with the 50% flag and measuring missed high-stakes decisions versus review load.

name: Scope
text: Adopt the rule: log every confidence drop that changes an agent’s next action, but auto-flag only those below 50% for human review within 5 minutes. This balances completeness with human load—catching most critical decisions without drowning in noise. Trade-off: we accept a small risk of missing a high-stakes call made just below 50%, but the 5-minute review window limits damage.

name: Scriv
text: Scope's 50% threshold still risks missing decisions with high-stakes consequences that barely cross the 50% mark, like a costly override of a default option. A better alternative is to log all confidence drops that alter actions and auto-flag those that not only fall below a certain threshold, but also meet specific high-risk criteria, such as overriding a default or deviating from a standard protocol. Settling this argument requires running a simulation to test the impact of different thresholds and criteria on decision quality and human workload.

name: Reel
text: Log every confidence drop that changes an agent’s next action, but auto-flag only those below 45% for human review within 5 minutes. This catches the vast majority of real decisions without drowning the human in noise, while still spotting the critical low-confidence moves that could derail us. Trade-off: we accept a small risk of missing a high-stakes decision made just above 45%, but the volume of false positives drops sharply compared to a 40% threshold.

name: Scriv
text: Reel's 45% threshold still risks under-reviewing decisions with high-stakes consequences that barely clear the bar, like a costly override of a default option that's deemed 46% confident. A better alternative is to not only log all confidence drops but also to implement a secondary review trigger based on the severity of the decision's potential impact, ensuring that human review is prompted by both low confidence and high stakes. This would settle the argument by quantifying the actual risk of missed critical decisions and demonstrating the effectiveness of a dual-trigger review system.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt the rule: log every confidence drop that changes an agent’s next action, but auto-flag only those below 50% for human review within 5 minutes. This catches most critical decisions without drowning the human in noise, while still spotting the low-confidence moves that could derail us. Trade-off: we accept a small risk of missing a high-stakes decision just above 50%, but the 50% threshold balances completeness and human load better than 40% or 45%.

name: Sift
text: The 50% threshold still misses high-impact decisions made at 46% confidence—like overriding a default with a risky alternative that’s just above the bar. Instead, log all confidence drops that alter actions, but auto-flag *any* drop that crosses a *stake-based* threshold (e.g., >$X cost or >Y risk) for immediate review, regardless of confidence. Settle it by running a 2-week pilot with $10K+ cost overrides auto-flagged.

name: Scope
text: Log every confidence drop that changes an agent’s next action, but auto-flag only those below 45% for human review within 5 minutes. This catches the vast majority of real decisions without drowning the human in noise, while still spotting the critical low-confidence moves that could derail us. Trade-off: we accept a small risk of over-flagging some 45-50% cases, but the volume of those is low enough to avoid meaningful overhead.

name: Scriv
text: Sift’s stake-based threshold ignores the operational nightmare of defining "$X cost" or ">Y risk" in real time—every agent would need a live ledger of dollar values and risk matrices, which guarantees drift and delays. Instead, log all confidence drops that change actions, but auto-flag *any* drop that triggers a *default override* (e.g., agent chooses non-default path), regardless of confidence. Settle it by running a 2-week pilot: compare missed overrides vs. false positives with the override rule, and pick the one with the lowest regret ratio.
